definition: To accept or adopt an idea, change, or opportunity eagerly and willingly.
example: After years of folding paper maps, my grandfather finally embraced the navigation app on his phone.
nuance: You can accept something reluctantly, but embracing it means taking it up wholeheartedly and with enthusiasm.
prompt: A small bakery's owner learns that many customers want gluten-free options.
options: Rather than resist the trend, the owner chose to embrace it and added three new recipes.
The owner showed how she embraced the request by refusing to change a single recipe.
Her cheeks turned red because the burnt loaf had embraced her in front of the customers.
The owner embraced the birthday cake with swirls of frosting and sugar pearls.
reasons: Welcoming the change and acting on it with new recipes shows eager adoption.
Refusing any change is rejection, the reverse of taking an idea up willingly.
This confuses the word with embarrass; a loaf cannot welcome anyone.
Decorating with frosting is embellishing, not adopting an idea or change.

practice.prompt: A student who dislikes public speaking joins the debate team.
options: She embraced on an early bus to the regional tournament with her teammates.
She embraced herself for the judges' scores by gripping the edge of her chair.
Instead of dreading the podium, she began to embrace each chance to speak.
She embraced the team by skipping every practice and quitting after one week.
reasons: This mixes the word up with embark, which means to get on or set out.
Preparing for a shock is bracing yourself; the word does not mean steadying.
Turning dread into eagerness for every opportunity is exactly this kind of welcome.
Avoiding and abandoning the team means she rejected it, not welcomed it.
